# Where is the sun in this picture of the ruined peristyle house?

## The answer in one paragraph

The sun is **off the frame beyond the top-left corner: high up and away to the left of the
camera.** In bearing it sits roughly **60–75° round to the left of the direction the lens
is pointing** — i.e. not just past the left border of the picture, but another 30–40°
beyond it, almost at right angles to the line of sight and tilted slightly *forward*
(towards the far side of the ruin) rather than backwards. In height it is **very high,
about 65–75° above the horizon, only some 15–25° short of the zenith.** Because the camera
is tilted about 20° downwards to look into the courtyard, the visible top edge of the
frame is essentially at horizon level, so a sun that high lies a very long way above the
picture. Put together, the sun's direction is a little more than a right angle away from
the lens axis, which places it **high up and just behind the photographer's left
shoulder.** That is precisely why it cannot be seen: it is outside the top-left of the
field of view.

## How the visible shadows support this

**1. Every cast shadow on the ground runs to the RIGHT and slightly DOWNWARD in the
frame.** Look at the foot of the column standing on the right-hand side of the courtyard
(just left of the ruined wall, about two-thirds of the way across the picture): a short,
dark shadow spills out of its base onto the pale flagstones, heading to the right and
dipping a little towards the bottom of the frame. The same happens at the two columns of
the left-hand colonnade: a stubby dark bar lies on the grass and kerbstone on the
right-hand side of each base. Shadows always point directly away from the sun, so the
sun must be on the **left**. The slight downward (towards-the-viewer) tilt of the shadows
means the sun is not exactly abeam of the camera but a little **in front** of it, which is
why the bearing works out at about 60–75° rather than a full 90°.

**2. Every cylindrical column is lit on its left flank and shaded on its right flank.**
On the shafts and on the moulded torus bases, the stone is bright cream/pale gold on the
left and falls away into brown-grey shadow on the right. The terminator on a vertical
cylinder sits 90° round from the light, so this puts the light squarely off to the left.

**3. The lit strip on the tall isolated column is very narrow, which shows the sun is far
round to the left.** On the slender column standing alone in front of the courtyard
(left-of-centre, rising above the foreground wall), only a thin ribbon down its left edge
catches the sun; almost the whole camera-facing side of the shaft is in shade. A cylinder
only looks like that when the light is coming from close to 90° round from the viewer —
strong side/back-left lighting, not light over the photographer's shoulder from straight
behind.

**4. Shadows thrown onto vertical surfaces are displaced to the right of whatever casts
them.** In the roofless rooms beyond the courtyard, the tapering brick piers each have a
bright cream left face and throw a dark, pier-shaped patch of shadow onto the masonry

the left, and it is independent of the ground slope.

ones are lit.** The long wall on the right of the frame has a dazzling white top course of

deep shade for the same reason. Likewise, the courtyard-facing (lower-right-facing) side

range from behind it.

**6. The shadows are extremely short, so the sun is nearly overhead.** The column shadows
are only about a third of the columns' height once the severe foreshortening of the ground
plane in this high, oblique viewpoint is allowed for — that corresponds to a solar altitude
of roughly 70°. Everything that is consistent with a near-vertical sun is visible here:
the courtyard lawn is almost entirely sunlit, with no long bars of shadow thrown across it
by the surrounding colonnade; the brightest surfaces in the whole picture are the
horizontal ones (wall tops, broken column drums, the flagstones of the alley); and the
shadows hug the feet of their objects instead of streaming away from them.

The horizon in the picture is the distant plain across the very top of the frame, only
about 5% of the way down. That tells you the camera is tilted roughly 20° below horizontal.
Take the shadow directions measured at the column bases, correct them for the perspective
of the ground plane, and extend them backwards: the parallel shadow lines converge on a
point on the horizon well **off the left edge** of the picture, about 60–75° round from the
camera's heading. Combine that bearing with the ~70° altitude implied by the shadow
lengths, and the resulting direction lies about 95–105° away from the optical axis —
just past a right angle. So the sun is not merely a bit beyond the left border; it is high
above and marginally behind the camera, off the **upper-left**, out of shot.

hilltop site like this (roughly 36°N), with the spring vegetation shown — lush green grass,
yellow and red wildflowers — that is about as high as the sun ever gets. If the sun is
therefore in the southern sky, the camera must be looking roughly west-south-west, with the
sun away to its left in the south. That compass reading is a reasonable inference rather
than something the shadows alone can prove; what the shadows do establish firmly is the
sun's position *relative to the frame*: off-picture, far to the left and very high.
